第 18 章 Do Less, Lead More做得更少，领导更多

Katie Womersley / 凯蒂·沃姆斯利

— 第 61 页 —

There comes a time for every engineering manager when you just can't do all of the things you need to do. This might be when you first switch to management, and you try to do one-on-ones, lead planning and scoping, figure out performance reviews, and still keep your hands in the code. It comes again later when you first start managing two teams and your workload doubles—even though you do not. It might happen when you need to fill more than one role, or when your startup hits a growth spurt. If you're a leader, this will happen, and it will happen often. If you're ambitious, you want this to happen. Managers level up when they successfully widen their sphere of influence, so you need to learn how to lead more when you can't simply do more.

每个工程经理都会有一个时刻，你就是做不完所有要做的事。可能是你刚转管理时，你试着做一对一、领导计划和范围界定、搞绩效评估，同时还把手放在代码里。后来你第一次管两个团队时又会遇到——工作量翻倍了——但你没有。可能发生在你需要身兼数职时，或者创业公司快速扩张时。如果你是领导，这种事会发生，而且经常发生。如果你有野心，你希望它发生。经理成功扩大影响力范围时就升级了，所以你需要学会在不能简单地做更多时，如何领导更多。

This is also when most engineering managers fail. You do the logical thing: write up a list of everything that must be done (and you know what must get done; you've been doing it!). You prioritize that list somehow, usually in order of what's on fire right now, and then smash through that list until the wee hours. You sleep too little and repeat the cycle. You get tetchy, make poor decisions, and "clean up yesterday's mess" starts getting added to tomorrow's TODO list. It does not end well.

这也是大多数工程经理失败的时候。你做了逻辑上的事：写下所有必须做的事的清单（你知道什么必须完成；你一直在做！）。你以某种方式排优先级，通常按现在什么在着火来排，然后猛冲清单直到凌晨。你睡得太少，然后重复循环。你变得暴躁，做出糟糕的决定，「清理昨天的烂摊子」开始被加到明天的待办列表里。结局不好。

Big changes call for desperate measures. The mistake here is trying to do everything that must be done, because you think you can do it. You're wrong. Sooner or later, something will slip, and the chances are, it will be something important that never reached urgent status. Instead of letting your failures pick you, you must explicitly choose what you will let fail. Intentionally not doing certain tasks is a manager super power. The best leaders learn this early and rely on this skill often.

大变革需要非常手段。这里的错误是试图做所有必须做的事，因为你觉得你能做到。你错了。迟早会有事情掉链子，而且很可能是那些从未变成紧急但很重要的事。不要让失败选择你，你必须明确选择你让什么失败。故意不做某些事是经理的超能力。最好的领导者很早就学到这一点，并且经常依赖这个技能。

— 第 62 页 —

A common example of needing to choose what to let go so that you don't find yourself accidentally losing sight of something critical occurs when you step up to lead two teams for the first time. This is often the first management step up, and you need to change how you operate because you won't have enough hours to lead both teams in the same way you led your one previous team. To attempt that would mean doing everything badly. Instead, figure out which team really needs to succeed, and which initiatives really need your personal guidance.

一个常见例子是：当你第一次开始领导两个团队时，需要选择放手什么，以免不小心忽略关键事项。这通常是第一次管理晋升，你需要改变运作方式，因为你没有足够的时间像之前带一个团队那样带两个团队。试图那样做意味着每件事都做不好。相反，搞清楚哪个团队真正需要成功、哪些举措真正需要你的亲自指导。

If you had to report back to your own manager that one of these teams is off track or one subproject is slipping, what would you rather be sharing bad news about? Use this "bad news test" to identify what you can delegate and who on your team is competent and eager to take on the extra responsibility. For example, you might do shorter one-on-ones or fewer skip-level one-on-ones, and you might delegate leading standups to a senior engineer. Or, you might pause or delegate your project to revamp the engineering onboarding process.

如果你必须向自己的经理汇报其中一个团队偏离轨道或某个子项目在延误，你更愿意汇报哪个坏消息？用这个「坏消息测试」来识别你可以授权什么、团队里谁有能力且渴望承担额外责任。例如，你可以缩短一对一时间或减少跨级一对一，把主持站会授权给高级工程师。或者，你可以暂停或授权你改造工程入职流程的项目。

After you've delegated the things that can more safely fail, focus your efforts on the things that (really) can't fail. This is a small subset of the things you think you "must" do. Choose wisely and choose few. Don't let this list expand, or you'll be again making an implicit choice about what will fall through the cracks. Make sure to share what you expect will slip with anyone who will be affected as well as with anyone who might help.

授权了那些可以更安全地失败的事情之后，把精力集中在（真正）不能失败的事情上。这是你认为「必须」做的事情的一小部分。明智地选择，选少一点。不要让这个清单扩大，否则你又在隐含地选择什么会掉地上。确保和所有受影响的人以及可能帮忙的人分享你预计会延误什么。

The worst thing you can do here is secretly let things slide, because you're ashamed of having priorities. Priorities are vital! Share openly what your responsibilities and goals are, the outcomes that you are choosing to prioritize, and the changes that you'll make. Tell your stakeholders clearly what has been delegated, deprioritized, or simply won't get done.

你在这里能做的最糟糕的事是偷偷让事情滑过去，因为你为自己有优先级而感到羞愧。优先级是至关重要的！公开分享你的责任和目标是什么、你选择优先考虑什么结果、以及你会做什么改变。清楚地告诉利益相关方什么被授权了、什么被降低优先级了、或者什么根本不会做。

Telling people what you're not doing achieves two things. First, it builds trust that you made an intentional decision—you have not simply forgotten. Second, and more important, by pairing your own prioritization with delegating these tasks to developing leaders on your team, it creates room for others to level up along with you. The best leaders take what they say no to, and use that as an opportunity to create a growth opportunity for someone else.

告诉人们你不做什么能达到两个效果。第一，它建立了信任——你是有意做的决定，不是忘了。第二，也是更重要的，通过把你自己的优先级排序和把这些任务授权给团队中成长中的领导者结合起来，为别人和你一起升级创造了空间。最好的领导者把他们说「不」的事情，用作给别人创造成长机会的机会。

If you do this successfully, you'll not only deliver what really matters. You'll also have leveled up your team and scaled yourself by increasing the leadership of those around you. Before you know it, you'll be promoted—and the intense growth cycle will begin again.

如果你成功做到这一点，你不仅交付了真正重要的东西。你还升级了你的团队、通过提升周围人的领导力扩展了你自己。不知不觉中，你就会被晋升——然后那个紧张的成长循环又会重新开始。
